repos.name: morluto / rea
repos.description: Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries.

summary.goal: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and CLI that connects coding agents to tools for reverse-engineering native binaries, JavaScript/Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites.
summary.usage: Run `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA with a supported agent and install matching workflow instructions; analysis then runs locally. For a quick terminal-only result on an extracted app, run `npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json`, which needs no MCP setup, Hopper, or Ghidra.
summary.pros: Static JavaScript/Electron analysis requires only the Node/npm runtime, and all analysis runs locally rather than uploading the app to a hosted service. Returned results include inline Evidence plus stated limitations and unknowns.
summary.cons: Deep native binary analysis depends on a separately licensed and installed engine — Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA Pro — none of which REA downloads or bundles; Hopper's demo mode carries vendor-defined limits. Native Windows support (via Ghidra) is still described as experimental.
summary.fit: REA documents support for agents including Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Devin, OpenCode, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot CLI, Command Code, and VS Code, suggesting it suits teams already working with agentic coding tools. Given the external-engine prerequisites for deep native analysis, it may fit developers comfortable with some local tool configuration better than those wanting a fully turnkey setup.

repos.name: mattpocock / skills
repos.description: Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

summary.goal: Skills For Real Engineers (mattpocock/skills) is a collection of agent skills intended for everyday real engineering work with coding agents, rather than casual "vibe coding."
summary.usage: Install the skill set either as a managed Claude Code plugin with `claude plugins install mattpocock-skills`, or as editable files via skills.sh with `npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills`. Either way, run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` once per repository to configure the issue tracker, triage labels, and documentation location before using the other skills.
summary.pros: The skills are described as small, easy to adapt, composable, and compatible with any model. They target specific failure modes seen with coding agents, including misalignment on requirements, excessive verbosity, unreliable code from weak feedback loops, and architectural decay over time.
summary.cons: Updates delivered through the Claude Code plugin marketplace can lag behind this repository's releases by days or weeks, and installing both the plugin and skills.sh methods results in every skill being duplicated. The improve-codebase-architecture skill is also described only as a survey tool that identifies refactoring candidates, not one that resolves codebase complexity on its own.
summary.fit: This project appears aimed at engineers working with Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding agents who want repeatable, structured workflows spanning both engineering tasks (such as code review, TDD, and architecture review) and general productivity tasks (such as interviews and handoff documents).

repos.name: boykopovar / AnyPS5
repos.description: Tool for automatic PS5 executables porting to Linux and Windows

summary.goal: AnyPS5 is a tool for automatically porting executables to Linux and Windows. It includes a relinker that converts executables to the target system's native format, plus implementations of system PRX libraries for dynamic linking, without emulation or a separate runtime process.
summary.usage: Usage instructions are documented in docs/user/USAGE.md, with build instructions in docs/dev/BUILD.md. Keyboard and mouse controls can be configured via an anyps5-input.ini file, and SDL-mapped game controllers, including analog sticks and triggers, are supported.
summary.pros: Dreaming Sarah, a 2D platformer, is reported to run at a stable 60 fps on a GTX 1050 Ti / i5-7500 3.4GHz setup. The shader recompiler successfully produces SPIR-V output, which can be validated via SPIRV-Tools when built with the ANYPS5_ENABLE_SPIRV_TOOLS flag.
summary.cons: Unsupported or unexpected states throw a std::runtime_error, print the error to stderr, and terminate the process, which suggests limited graceful error recovery. System library coverage is also tracked only as a percentage of functions known to the project so far rather than the full PS5 API, implying compatibility work appears to still be ongoing.
summary.fit: The project targets interoperability, research, preservation, and compatibility purposes, stating it does not include or require copyrighted software, firmware, cryptographic keys, or proprietary libraries. It is distributed under the GNU General Public License version 2 only, so users must ensure any binaries used comply with applicable laws and licenses.

repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd
repos.description: A skill to stop your coding agent from burying the answer. ADHD-friendly output.

summary.goal: i-have-adhd is a skill/plugin for coding assistants that reshapes their responses to lead with the next action, number multi-step tasks, and drop filler phrases like "Hope this helps!".
summary.usage: Install i-have-adhd by pasting the documented command referencing https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd and AGENTS.md into a CLI prompt, or follow INSTALL.md; to customize, fork the repo, edit skills/i-have-adhd/SKILL.md, then run commands such as `claude plugin install i-have-adhd@i-have-adhd` to swap in the forked copy.
summary.pros: The i-have-adhd skill defines 10 explicit rules—leading with the next action, numbering steps, capping lists to 5 items, and removing preamble/recap/closers—illustrated by a before/after example contrasting a meandering answer with a direct, numbered one.
summary.cons: Customizing i-have-adhd requires forking the repository and running several plugin commands (`claude plugin uninstall i-have-adhd`, `claude plugin marketplace remove i-have-adhd`, then re-adding and installing under the fork), since the README notes the fork and upstream share the same name; this suggests the tuning workflow may be tied to the Claude plugin command set rather than a single simple step.
summary.fit: i-have-adhd fits users of coding assistants who want concise, action-first, numbered responses regardless of an ADHD diagnosis; it is released under the MIT license and is loosely adapted from the book The Adult ADHD Tool Kit for how an LLM should respond, not for personal day organization.

repos.name: cathrynlavery / diagram-design
repos.description: Editorial diagram design for Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Factory Droid, and Pi. 42 diagram types. Self-contained HTML + SVG. No shadows. No Mermaid slop.

summary.goal: diagram-design is an Agent Skill that generates editorial-style diagrams (architecture, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and dozens of other layout types) as self-contained HTML+SVG files for Claude Code, Codex, Factory Droid, Pi, and other Agent Skills-compatible hosts, aiming to replace generic Mermaid output or manual Figma work.
summary.usage: Install via a host-specific plugin command; in Claude Code this is `/plugin marketplace add cathrynlavery/diagram-design` followed by `/plugin install diagram-design@diagram-design`, while hosts without a dedicated marketplace can run `npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design`. Once installed, diagrams can be requested in natural language, and existing draw.io, Mermaid, or Excalidraw files can be imported and redrawn.
summary.pros: The skill ships a large set of diagram types (architecture, ER, sequence, Sankey, Wardley maps, and more added through version 2.5.10), includes accessibility features such as ARIA labeling by default, and can automatically match a project's brand colors and fonts by reading a target website during a brief onboarding flow.
summary.cons: Exporting diagrams to PNG requires a one-time local setup step, `pip install playwright && playwright install chromium`, and directly customizing the style guide may be overwritten by later package updates unless an editable (cloned) install is used instead of a managed plugin install.
summary.fit: This likely fits teams already working inside Claude Code, Codex, Factory Droid, Pi, or similar Agent Skills hosts who want on-brand, editorial-quality diagrams rather than generic boxes; the documentation suggests it is not intended for quick unicode diagrams, simple lists, or single-box visuals, which are better served by plain text or tables.

repos.name: addyosmani / agent-skills
repos.description: Production-grade engineering skills for AI coding agents.

summary.goal: Agent Skills is a collection of 25 production-grade engineering skills packaged for AI coding agents, covering the full development lifecycle from spec to shipping. It encodes workflows, quality gates, and best practices that senior engineers use, so agents can follow them consistently.
summary.usage: Install all skills with `npx skills add addyosmani/agent-skills`, or install into Claude Code via `/plugin marketplace add addyosmani/agent-skills` followed by `/plugin install agent-skills@addy-agent-skills`. Nine slash commands (e.g. `/spec`, `/build`, `/test`, `/review`, `/ship`) map to lifecycle stages.
summary.pros: The CLI reportedly installs into 70+ agents including Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Copilot, and skills activate automatically based on the task at hand, such as API design or UI work. Nine commands streamline the lifecycle without manual skill selection.
summary.cons: Installing a single skill via npx copies only that skill's folder, not the shared `references/` directory, so supplementary checklists become unavailable unless a whole-repo install or manual copy is used; this portability gap is tracked as issue #361.
summary.fit: The pack appears suited for teams using AI coding agents who want consistent spec-driven, tested, and reviewed workflows across multiple tools; Claude Code is noted as the recommended integration, with native support also described for Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and others.

repos.name: EpicGames / raddebugger
repos.description: A native, user-mode, multi-process, graphical debugger.

summary.goal: The RAD Debugger project (EpicGames/raddebugger) provides a native, user-mode, multi-process, graphical debugger for local-machine Windows x64 debugging with PDB files, alongside two related technologies: the RAD Debug Info (RDI) format and the RAD Linker. The project is currently labeled ALPHA.
summary.usage: On Windows, run `build` from the codebase root in an MSVC/Clang-enabled terminal, or `build release` for an optimized build. On Linux, run `./build.sh` or `./build.sh release`. Pre-built release binaries are also available at https://github.com/EpicGames/raddebugger/releases.
summary.pros: In the project's own test cases, the RAD Linker reports 50% faster link times than prior approaches on huge, debug-info-heavy projects, with an additional 25% reduction available when large memory pages are explicitly enabled. Its command-line syntax is described as fully MSVC-compatible.
summary.cons: The debugger currently only supports local-machine Windows x64 debugging with PDB debug info; Linux and DWARF support are planned but not yet implemented, and the project is explicitly in ALPHA. Large memory page support for the RAD Linker is off by default because Windows handling of large pages can be unreliable, potentially fragmenting memory and forcing a reboot, so it is recommended mainly for Docker or VM environments.
summary.fit: This project likely suits teams needing native Windows x64 PDB debugging and performance-focused linking for very large C/C++ projects, though its alpha status and current Windows-only debugging scope suggest it may not yet fit teams requiring Linux debugging or DWARF-based toolchains.

repos.name: thedotmack / claude-mem
repos.description: Persistent Context Across Sessions for Every Agent –  Captures everything your agent does during sessions, compresses it with AI, and injects relevant context back into future sessions. Works with Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot, OpenCode + More

summary.goal: Claude-Mem (currently version 13.34.2) is a persistent memory compression system built for Claude Code. It automatically captures tool usage observations, generates semantic summaries, and makes that context available across future sessions, so Claude can maintain continuity of project knowledge after a session ends or reconnects.
summary.usage: Install it with `npx claude-mem install`, or add it from the Claude Code plugin marketplace via `/plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem` and `/plugin install claude-mem`. After installation, restart Claude Code and prior session context appears automatically in new sessions. Full documentation is available at https://docs.claude-mem.ai/.
summary.pros: Key features include persistent memory across sessions, progressive disclosure of context with token-cost visibility, a skill-based mem-search tool, a web viewer UI, privacy controls via `<private>` tags, and automatic operation without manual intervention. It also exposes 4 MCP search tools following a 3-layer workflow (search → timeline → get_observations) described as giving roughly 10x token savings by filtering before fetching full details.
summary.cons: It requires Node.js 20.0.0 or higher and a version of Claude Code with plugin support, along with Bun and uv runtimes (auto-installed if missing). Running the generic `npm install -g claude-mem` only installs the SDK/library and does not register plugin hooks or set up the worker service, so the dedicated installer is needed for full functionality. The hosted claude-mem observer memory includes a 30-day free trial, after which usage may fall back to the user's Anthropic plan unless they subscribe.
summary.fit: This tool is likely best suited to developers already using Claude Code or related harnesses (OpenCode, T3 Code, Antigravity CLI, Grok Bot) who want continuity of project context across sessions. It may be less suitable for users who prefer not to manage a local worker service, SQLite database, and vector-search dependencies that run alongside the host tool.

repos.name: manaflow-ai / cmux
repos.description: Open source Ghostty-based macOS terminal with vertical tabs and notifications for AI coding agents. Built for multitasking, organization, and programmability.

summary.goal: cmux is a native macOS terminal application built on Ghostty's rendering engine (libghostty), offering vertical and horizontal tabs, workspace management, and notifications for users running AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex in parallel panes.
summary.usage: Install the stable build by downloading the macOS DMG from GitHub releases, or via Homebrew with `brew tap manaflow-ai/cmux` followed by `brew install --cask cmux`; update later with `brew upgrade --cask cmux`. On first launch, macOS may require confirming the app came from an identified developer.
summary.pros: cmux is a native Swift/AppKit app rather than Electron, aimed at fast startup and low memory use. It reads an existing Ghostty config for themes and fonts, adds notification rings/panels when agents need attention, includes a scriptable in-app browser, SSH workspace support, and a CLI/socket API for automating workspaces and panes. The project is open source.
summary.cons: cmux currently supports macOS only, so it is not usable on Windows or Linux. Separately, while the cmux app itself is licensed GPL-3.0-or-later, its server components (the `web/` directory, Cloudflare workers, and relay services) use the Business Source License 1.1, meaning production use or self-hosting of those parts requires a commercial license.
summary.fit: The tool appears best suited to macOS developers who run multiple terminal-based AI coding agents and want built-in notifications and workspace visibility rather than a prescriptive orchestration product; it may be less relevant for users on other operating systems or those seeking an opinionated, GUI-driven workflow.

repos.name: trycua / cua
repos.description: Scale computer-use 2.0 with open-source drivers, cross-OS fleets, and benchmarks for training, evaluation, and data generation.

summary.goal: Cua is a repository that provides computer environments AI agents can use, bundling several related tools: Cua Spaces for full desktops on Mac and owned machines, Cua Driver for desktop automation on macOS, Windows, and Linux, Lume for local macOS/Linux virtual machines, CUA-S1 decision models for computer-use tasks, and Cua Bench for evaluating computer-use agents.
summary.usage: Cua Spaces and the Cua SDK/CLI can be installed on macOS or Linux with `curl -fsSL https://cua.ai/install.sh | sh`, which also adds the `cua` command-line tool. Sandboxes can then be created with commands such as `cua sb create ubuntu --name dev`, or managed from Python via the cua_sandbox library.
summary.pros: The README states Cua Spaces is free for individuals, the project offers the same SDK API across Python, TypeScript, Swift, and Kotlin, and Cua Driver supports macOS, Windows, and Linux.
summary.cons: Several packages, including cuabot, cua-computer, cua-computer-server, cua-agent, and cua-som, are explicitly marked deprecated and will not receive further updates; the README additionally states cuabot has known security issues and should not be run.
summary.fit: The project may suit developers building or evaluating AI agents that need desktop-level automation or sandboxed environments, though Cua Spaces requires macOS 26 or later and some components, such as CUA-S1, are described as an early, source-only research release.

repos.name: cloudflare / security-audit-skill
repos.description: A coding-agent skill for multi-phase security audits with independently verified, machine-readable findings

summary.goal: This is a coding-agent skill that turns an agent into a security auditor, running a structured six-phase audit: reconnaissance, coverage-led hunting, candidate validation, structured output, independent record verification, and target-neutral reporting. It originated as the single-repo starting point for Cloudflare's vulnerability discovery harness.
summary.usage: Install with the Skills CLI: `npx skills add https://github.com/cloudflare/security-audit-skill --skill security-audit` (add `--global` for a user-level install). Then start a coding agent in the target codebase and issue a request such as `security audit this codebase`; matching triggers activate full audit mode, writing reports to `~/security-audit-skill/<repo-name>/run-<N>` by default.
summary.pros: Findings undergo adversarial validation, since the agent that checks a candidate is never the one that found it, and reports distinguish confirmed, needs_validation, and rejected verdicts. The findings and coverage-ledger validators are zero-dependency Node scripts. Documentation suggests that in test runs, repeated runs found roughly double the vulnerabilities a single run found.
summary.cons: The workflow requires Node.js for its validators and an OS-enforced sandbox that disables external networking, uses a sanitized allowlisted environment, enforces resource limits, and restricts writes to scratch paths for any target-controlled execution. Without such a sandbox, leads that need code execution remain marked needs_validation rather than being confirmed.
summary.fit: It is intended for coding agents whose underlying model supports tool use and parallel sub-agents, run against a codebase the user points it at. Multiple runs against the same repository are additive, reusing prior ledgers and findings to target coverage gaps rather than repeating prior work.

repos.name: tester-army / e2e
repos.description: Next generation e2e testing framework for web and mobile apps.

summary.goal: e2e is an end-to-end testing framework for web and mobile apps in which a user describes a goal in natural language and an agent drives the app to reach it, checking the result with locators and assertions in the same test (lines 14-16).
summary.usage: Setup starts with `npx e2e init`, which asks for an engine (web or mobile) and a model provider, then writes a config file and an example test; telemetry can be turned off with `npx e2e telemetry disable` (lines 40-43, 82-84).
summary.pros: Recorded agent steps are replayed without further model calls until the app changes, and tests with no agent steps need no model at all, which may help reduce ongoing model usage for stable test suites (lines 32-35).
summary.cons: The documentation explicitly states the project is in active development on the way to version 1.0, with APIs and config still subject to change between minor releases (lines 89-91).
summary.fit: Because it requires bringing a subscription, API key, or local model of one's own, e2e appears best suited to teams already using Node-based tooling who are comfortable integrating a model provider into their test pipeline (lines 34-35, 43).

repos.name: DuarteSantos8 / openGym
repos.description: Self-hosted gym & body-weight tracker — plan routines, log workouts (supersets, warm-ups, cardio), see which muscles are trained, fatigued or detrained, import from FitNotes/Strong/Hevy, passkey login. Your data, your server.

summary.goal: openGym is a self-hosted gym and body-weight tracker intended to run entirely under the user's control, syncing data across devices while keeping storage in a folder the user owns (lines 5-8, 41-44).
summary.usage: Setup follows `git clone https://github.com/DuarteSantos8/openGym`, then `docker compose up -d` inside the project folder; the app becomes reachable at http://localhost:8080, and the first launch downloads about 140 MB of exercise media once.
summary.pros: Documented capabilities include passkey sign-in with cross-device sync, a library of 1,324 searchable exercises, import support for FitNotes, Strong, Hevy and Apple Health data, and distribution under the AGPL v3.0 open-source license.
summary.cons: The exercise images and animations are explicitly stated as not covered by the AGPL license, with ownership disputed between Gym visual and ExerciseDB; reusing that media is described as requiring separate clearance from the rights holder.
summary.fit: Given its Docker-based self-hosting approach and stated absence from the Play Store, openGym appears best suited to users comfortable managing their own server rather than those seeking app-store-only installs, since iPhone users are told Apple does not allow installs outside the App Store.

repos.name: mvschwarz / openrig
repos.description: Build your own network of agents from Claude Code, Codex and Pi: persistent teams with roles, shared context and owned work.

summary.goal: OpenRig is open-source software for building and running a network of AI coding agents. It wraps model harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex into a managed "rig," letting users define agent teams declaratively in YAML and boot them with a single command.
summary.usage: Install OpenRig with one command, `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvschwarz/openrig/v0.6.6/scripts/install.sh | sh`, or step by step via `npm install -g @openrig/cli` followed by `rig setup`. It requires Node.js 22 or 24 and tmux, and runs on macOS or Linux.
summary.pros: OpenRig lets Claude Code and Codex operate within the same team, ships prebuilt teams (`starter`, `workshop`, `factory`) sized for different workloads, and provides a CLI, TUI, and MCP server built on tmux, so every agent session remains inspectable and attachable.
summary.cons: Launching a rig writes provider hooks and workspace trust settings to the user's machine, and the README advises backing up relevant files beforehand; it also notes that settings recovery is not a complete preservation or rollback guarantee, suggesting some configuration changes may not be fully reversible.
summary.fit: OpenRig is self-hosted, running on the user's own infrastructure with macOS or Linux and, for service-backed rigs, Docker, while model usage costs from the chosen providers apply separately; this points to a fit for users wanting persistent, self-managed coordination of multiple coding agents rather than a single disposable session.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes
repos.description: Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.

summary.goal: HyperFrames is an open-source (Apache 2.0) framework that converts HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. It can be used locally via a CLI, through AI coding-agent skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.
summary.usage: Scaffold a project with `npx hyperframes init my-video`, then `cd my-video` and run `npx hyperframes preview` to preview in-browser or `npx hyperframes render` to produce an MP4. Claude Code users can instead run `claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes` and `claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes`. Requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg.
summary.pros: Compositions are plain HTML with no React requirement or proprietary timeline format, the CLI is non-interactive by default for agent use, and rendering is deterministic (same input, same output) for CI and regression testing. There is no build step since an index.html composition plays as-is, animation is adapter-based (GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI), and licensing is Apache 2.0 with no per-render fees.
summary.cons: Cloning the full repository for development requires installing Git LFS to fetch about 240 MB of golden regression-test .mp4 baseline files, an extra setup step beyond a plain git clone. Separately, a non-interactive skill install without the `--skill` flag installs all 21 published skills instead of just the core set.
summary.fit: The project appears best suited to developers or teams building automated, agent-driven, or CI-integrated video pipelines who prefer authoring in HTML/CSS over React, since it is positioned as an alternative to Remotion's React-based model — though this suitability is a cautious inference rather than an explicit claim.

repos.name: cursor / plugins
repos.description: Cursor plugin specification and official plugins

summary.goal: Cursor plugins is a repository of official plugins for developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products, each defined as a standalone directory with its own .cursor-plugin/plugin.json manifest.
summary.usage: The repository is structured as a multi-plugin marketplace: a root .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json lists all plugins, while each plugin directory contains its own manifest plus optional skills, rules, and mcp.json files.
summary.pros: The repository bundles a wide range of plugins across Developer Tools, Productivity, and Integrations categories, including connectors for tools such as GitHub, Google Drive, Salesforce, HubSpot, and QuickBooks Online.
summary.cons: Setting up or enabling a specific plugin likely requires working directly within that plugin's own directory, since the root structure only centralizes the marketplace listing and manifest discovery rather than a unified installation or CLI command.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for developers and teams building or extending Cursor agent workflows who want ready-made integrations with existing SaaS and developer tools, rather than those seeking a single standalone application.

repos.name: NVIDIA / OpenShell
repos.description: OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for autonomous AI agents.

summary.goal: OpenShell is described as a runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents that enforces kernel-level policy on file access, system calls, and network connections, and uses formal verification to review policy changes before they take effect.
summary.usage: Installation starts with `curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh`, followed by `openshell sandbox create --name demo` to create a sandbox. The default sandbox image is a minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed.
summary.pros: Each agent runs isolated so kernel controls restrict file and system-call access, and credentials are injected only into requests bound for approved endpoints rather than exposed directly to agents. Collected telemetry is limited to anonymous operational categories and counts, and can be disabled via an environment variable or a Helm setting.
summary.cons: Running OpenShell requires Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (marked experimental in the README), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. Deploying on Kubernetes additionally requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy.
summary.fit: Given the described policy-enforcement and credential-scoping features, OpenShell appears suited for teams operating multiple autonomous AI agents that need controlled file, network, and credential access, with deployment options spanning a local CLI or Kubernetes via Helm.

repos.name: Panniantong / Agent-Reach
repos.description: Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

summary.goal: Agent Reach is an open-source capability layer (MIT licensed, Python 3.10+) that gives AI agents shell-command access to internet platforms such as web pages, YouTube, RSS, GitHub, Twitter/X, Bilibili, and Reddit, by selecting, installing, and health-checking the most stable backend for each platform.
summary.usage: Users ask their AI agent (e.g. Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor) to run a one-line install instruction pointing to https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/install.md. By default this only checks the environment; `agent-reach install --system` is needed to install dependencies and write configuration. The `agent-reach doctor` command reports which backend each platform is currently using.
summary.pros: All tools and APIs are described as free and open source, aside from an optional server proxy costing about $1/month; credentials and cookies are stored only locally; installation defaults to a read-only check that does not modify the system; and each platform routes through an ordered list of backends so a broken integration can be swapped without reconfiguring the agent.
summary.cons: Several platforms (Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, Xiaohongshu, and advanced Twitter/LinkedIn features) require manual login or cookie configuration rather than working out of the box, and Reddit specifically has no zero-configuration path since its anonymous API access is blocked. The README also warns that cookie-based login on these platforms risks account suspension and recommends using dedicated secondary accounts rather than a primary one.
summary.fit: Based on the documented compatibility list, Agent Reach appears best suited to developers already using shell-capable AI agents like Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor, or Windsurf who want broader web/social-platform access without building per-platform integrations themselves; it is not a standalone scraping tool, since actual data fetching is still performed by the agent calling upstream tools directly.

repos.name: pablostanley / yoinks
repos.description: yoink any video from your terminal. no shady ads.

summary.goal: yoinks is a command-line tool for downloading videos and audio from YouTube, X/Twitter, Instagram, Threads, TikTok, and over 1,800 other sites. Users paste a URL, select a resolution or an audio-only mp3, and the file is saved locally.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npm install -g yoinks`, or run it once without installing via `npx yoinks`. Node 18+ is required. Launch with a URL (e.g. `yoinks <url>`) or run `yoinks` alone to be prompted for one; `--theme light` or `--theme dark` sets the starting color theme.
summary.pros: The tool avoids popups, fake download buttons, and redirects common on download sites. Its default theme automatically matches the terminal's own foreground and background colors. Dependencies such as yt-dlp and ffmpeg are fetched or bundled automatically, so a separate Python or ffmpeg installation is not documented as necessary.
summary.cons: Node 18+ is a stated prerequisite. According to the project's roadmap, several capabilities are not yet implemented, including flags for skipping the format picker, choosing an output directory, playlist support, clipboard detection, and a self-updating yt-dlp binary, suggesting that current scriptable and automation options are limited.
summary.fit: yoinks appears best suited to personal, interactive archiving of individual videos from supported platforms, with an explicit note that downloading may violate a platform's terms of service. It may be less suited to automated or batch downloading workflows for now, since related flags are still only planned.

repos.name: tile-ai / tilelang
repos.description: Domain-specific language designed to streamline the development of high-performance GPU/CPU/Accelerators kernels

summary.goal: TileLang (tile-lang) is a domain-specific language with Pythonic syntax for writing high-performance GPU/CPU/NPU kernels such as GEMM, FlashAttention, and LinearAttention, built on TVM compiler infrastructure.
summary.usage: Install via `pip install tilelang`; verify with `python -c "import tilelang; print(tilelang.__version__)"`. Kernels are defined with `@tilelang.jit` and `T.Kernel`/`T.gemm` primitives, as shown in the quickstart GEMM+ReLU example using PyTorch CUDA tensors.
summary.pros: Supports multiple backends (CUDA as primary, ROCm/HIP, Ascend 950, Apple Metal as supported tiers), with reported benchmark results on H100, A100, MI300X, and RTX 4090 GPUs, and frequent recent releases adding features like the LLVM backend and autotuning.
summary.cons: TileLang v0.1.13 removed several legacy APIs, so upgrading requires reviewing compatibility notes; ROCm/HIP support additionally requires a separately installed host ROCm runtime.
summary.fit: Appears suited for developers building custom GPU/NPU kernels for deep learning workloads such as attention and GEMM who need PyTorch interoperability and can target CUDA, ROCm, or Ascend hardware.

repos.name: HunxByts / GhostTrack
repos.description: Useful tool to track location or mobile number

summary.goal: GhostTrack is an OSINT (open-source intelligence) and information-gathering tool for tracking a target's location or mobile phone number. It is currently at version 2.2 and provides this functionality through IP Tracker, Phone Tracker, and Username Tracker menu options.
summary.usage: Setup requires git and python3, installed via apt-get on Linux or pkg on Termux. Users then run `git clone https://github.com/HunxByts/GhostTrack.git`, `cd GhostTrack`, `pip3 install -r requirements.txt`, and `python3 GhostTR.py` to launch the tool, which presents IP Tracker, Phone Tracker, and Username Tracker menu options.
summary.pros: The tool bundles three distinct tracking features (IP, phone number, and username lookup) in one menu-driven interface, and the IP Tracker can be combined with the external Seeker tool for extended target IP information.
summary.cons: Combining IP tracking with Seeker requires installing that separate third-party tool from its own repository, since Seeker is not bundled with GhostTrack. The README also does not document supported platforms beyond Linux (deb-based) and Termux.
summary.fit: Based on its documented features, GhostTrack appears best suited to OSINT or information-gathering tasks involving phone numbers, usernames, or IP addresses, for users comfortable running Python3 command-line tools on Linux or Termux.

repos.name: alibaba / open-code-review
repos.description: Secure, fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

summary.goal: Open Code Review is an AI-powered code review CLI tool that originated as Alibaba Group's internal review assistant before being open-sourced. It reads Git diffs and sends changed files to a configurable LLM through an agent with tool-use capabilities, producing structured, line-level review comments; `ocr scan` extends this to full-file review for codebases without a meaningful diff.
summary.usage: Install with `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`, then configure a provider and model, and run `ocr review` for diff-based reviews of staged/branch/commit changes or `ocr scan` to review entire files or directories.
summary.pros: Per the README's benchmark (50 repositories, 200 pull requests, 10 languages, 1,505 annotated issues), the tool reports higher precision and F1 than a general-purpose agent (Claude Code) on the same model while consuming about 1/9 of the tokens.
summary.cons: The README states Recall is lower than general-purpose agents, described as a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise; using the tool also requires Git >= 2.41 as a prerequisite.
summary.fit: It appears suited to teams wanting token-efficient, structured diff or full-file reviews via CLI or CI/CD, and its delegation mode reportedly lets a coding agent perform reviews without configuring an OCR-managed LLM, though this depends on the chosen execution mode.

repos.name: bilawalsidhu / gods-eye-view
repos.description: A spy satellite simulator in your browser, except the data is real. Live open source spatial intelligence on a photorealistic 3D globe.

summary.goal: God's Eye View is a browser-based 3D globe application that aggregates public, largely live data sources — aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, traffic, and public cameras — and adds voice control through a realtime AI agent.
summary.usage: Install via Pinokio, or run locally with Node.js 24.x (24.14.0 or later) or 26.x: `git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git`, then `npm ci` and `npm run dev`, opening `http://localhost:4173`. No API keys are required to start; optional keys (Cesium ion, Google Maps, OpenAI) can be added in-app for extra capabilities.
summary.pros: It runs without requiring an account or API keys, 17 of 19 documented data layers work keylessly, the source code is inspectable and released under the MIT License, and it supports voice-driven navigation and analyst-style queries over live layers.
summary.cons: Traffic is simulated along real roads from aggregate data rather than reflecting live vehicle positions, and CCTV camera poses are described as coarse estimates. The README also states the project is an evolving client, not a hardened production service, and notes that older Pinokio releases had an installation issue since addressed in version 8.2.
summary.fit: Based on the described feature set and documentation, this project appears best suited to developers, hobbyists, and learners exploring geospatial/OSINT-style visualization, since the README explicitly cautions against relying on it for navigation, emergency response, or other safety-critical decisions.

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC
repos.description: The agent harness performance optimization system. Skills, instincts, memory, security, and research-first development for Claude Code, Codex, Opencode, Cursor and beyond.

summary.goal: Claude for Financial Services provides reference agents, skills, and data connectors for financial-services workflows such as investment banking, equity research, private equity, and wealth management. It can be installed as a Claude Cowork plugin or deployed via the Claude Managed Agents API, using the same system prompt and skills in either case.
summary.usage: Add the marketplace with `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/financial-services`, then install a bundle such as `claude plugin install financial-analysis@claude-for-financial-services`. In Cowork, the repository URL `https://github.com/anthropics/financial-services` can instead be pasted under Settings → Plugins → Add plugin. Managed Agent deployment uses `scripts/deploy-managed-agent.sh gl-reconciler` after an API key is configured.
summary.pros: Agent plugins are self-contained, bundling the skills they need so installing one agent is sufficient. All data connectors (11 total) are centralized in the financial-analysis core plugin and shared across verticals, and both deployment paths reference the same system prompt and skills.
summary.cons: Some MCP connectors may require a subscription or API key from the provider, and subagent delegation (callable_agents) for Managed Agents is described as a research-preview capability. Outputs are also positioned as draft work product requiring review by a qualified professional before use.
summary.fit: This appears suited to financial firms wanting draft analyst work product—models, memos, reconciliations—staged for human sign-off rather than automated decision-making. It likely fits teams already using Claude Code or Cowork, or those able to deploy against the Managed Agents API with their own orchestration layer.

repos.name: paperclipai / paperclip
repos.description: The open-source app everyone uses to manage agents at work

summary.goal: Paperclip is open-source orchestration software — a Node.js server with a React UI — for managing teams of AI agents that run business work. It lets teams assign goals, bring their own agents, and track tasks, costs, and permissions from a single dashboard.
summary.usage: Paperclip is self-hosted and open source, requiring no Paperclip account. It can be installed and run with `npx paperclipai@latest onboard --yes` (Node.js 24.11 or newer), or by cloning the repository and running `pnpm install` followed by `pnpm dev`, which starts the UI and API at http://localhost:3100 with an automatically created embedded PostgreSQL database.
summary.pros: Documented capabilities include atomic task checkout that prevents duplicate work, budget and cost tracking with threshold alerts and automatic pauses, and support for multiple agent adapters such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and OpenClaw.
summary.cons: Building the native Paperclip Runner from source — enabled by default for self-hosted setups — requires installing a Rust toolchain, or alternatively setting the PAPERCLIP_RUNNER_BINARY variable to a compatible prebuilt runner, adding an extra setup step beyond Node.js and pnpm.
summary.fit: Paperclip is suited to teams coordinating many different agents toward shared goals, especially when they want to monitor costs and audit autonomous, long-running work; it is documented as not being an agent-building framework or prompt manager, but a system for managing the organization agents operate within.

repos.name: vectorize-io / hindsight
repos.description: Hindsight: Agent Memory That Learns

summary.goal: Hindsight is an agent memory system intended to help AI agents learn over time rather than only recall conversation history. The README reports state-of-the-art results on the LongMemEval benchmark, with performance data independently reproduced by Virginia Tech's Sanghani Center and The Washington Post.
summary.usage: Hindsight can be started via Docker (`docker run -it --pull always --name hindsight --restart unless-stopped -p 8888:8888 -p 9999:9999 ghcr.io/vectorize-io/hindsight:latest`), pip (`pip install hindsight-api`), Helm/Kubernetes, or the managed Hindsight Cloud. Clients in Python, Node.js, Go, CLI, or REST connect and call operations like `client.retain()`, `client.recall()`, and `client.reflect()`.
summary.pros: It documents support for 25+ LLM providers and 60+ integrations spanning coding agents, agent frameworks, and no-code tools. It also lists multilingual handling and an opt-in Memory Defense feature that scans retained content for secrets and PII; these appear to be documented capabilities rather than independently verified by us.
summary.cons: Deployment requires supplying an LLM API key and, for self-hosted setups, storage such as PostgreSQL or Oracle AI Database. Intel-based Macs reportedly need a separate `hindsight-all-slim` package for bare-metal installs, which suggests platform support is not fully uniform across architectures.
summary.fit: The README positions Hindsight for agents handling open-ended tasks and learning from feedback, such as AI employees, while noting it may be excessive for simpler workflows built with tools like n8n — suggesting it best suits more complex, long-running agent use cases.

summary.goal: Spotify Portal AI Plugins integrates Spotify Portal (https://portal.spotify.com) into Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, providing workflows built on the Portal CLI (@spotify/portal-cli) for authentication setup, software catalog search, service briefings, diagnostics, and invoking Portal actions.
summary.usage: Installation in Claude Code uses `claude plugin marketplace add spotify/portal-ai-plugins` followed by `claude plugin install portal@portal`, then running `/portal:setup` in a new session; the underlying Portal CLI is invoked via `npx @spotify/portal-cli <command>`.
summary.pros: Highlighted capabilities include CLI setup for the current coding-agent environment, read-only diagnostics (`doctor`) for plugin and authentication readiness, natural-language catalog and documentation search, concise service briefings, and action invocation with dry-run and confirmation safeguards.
summary.cons: The companion `shunt` plugin is described as Claude Code only 'for now,' which may suggest Codex and Cursor support could still be pending; the setup workflow also must first verify several required CLI commands (auth, actions, owner, search, service) before it can proceed.
summary.fit: Given its workflows center on Portal CLI operations like catalog search, service briefings, and action invocation, this project likely fits teams already using Spotify Portal who want those operations surfaced directly inside Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor sessions.

repos.name: Tencent / WeKnora
repos.description: Open-source LLM knowledge platform: turn raw documents into a queryable RAG, an autonomous reasoning agent, and a self-maintaining Wiki.

summary.goal: WeKnora is an open-source, LLM-powered knowledge framework from Tencent for enterprise document understanding, semantic retrieval and reasoning, combining RAG Q&A, a multi-step agent, and an automatic wiki over shared knowledge bases.
summary.usage: Deploy with Docker and Docker Compose: clone the repo, copy `.env.example` to `.env`, then run `docker compose pull` and `docker compose up -d`, and open http://localhost. A `weknora` CLI (e.g. `weknora kb list`, `weknora chat "..."`) and Kubernetes/Helm or a Lite single-binary mode are also documented.
summary.pros: It supports 27 built-in LLM vendors, multiple vector databases and storage backends, 10+ document formats, many data-source and IM integrations, and features like workspace RBAC, scoped API keys, and Langfuse tracing.
summary.cons: The README's security notice recommends deploying on an internal/private network with firewall controls rather than exposing it publicly, and warns that a plain `docker compose up -d` may leave the UI version out of sync with cached images during upgrades.
summary.fit: It appears best suited for teams needing a self-hostable or private-cloud knowledge/Q&A platform with document parsing and agent tooling, though the desktop app has no published installer yet and must be built from source.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-code
repos.description: Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that lives in your terminal, understands your codebase, and helps you code faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows - all through natural language commands.

summary.goal: Claude Code is presented as an agentic coding tool that lives in the terminal, understands a codebase, and helps developers work faster by executing routine tasks, explaining complex code, and handling git workflows through natural language commands. It can also be used inside an IDE or invoked on GitHub via @claude.
summary.usage: The README's recommended install method runs `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` on macOS/Linux (or `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex` on Windows), with Homebrew and WinGet also listed. After installing, users navigate to a project directory and run `claude` to start.
summary.pros: Documented strengths include natural-language handling of git workflows, code explanation, and routine task execution, plus flexibility across terminal, IDE, and GitHub (@claude) contexts. The repository also bundles several plugins that extend functionality with custom commands and agents.
summary.cons: The README marks npm installation (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`) as deprecated in favor of the curl/PowerShell/Homebrew/WinGet methods, so existing npm-based setups may need migration. Node.js 18+ appears required per the repository badge, though this is not restated in the running text.
summary.fit: Given its terminal-based, natural-language design and Node.js 18+ badge, Claude Code appears best suited to developers comfortable working from a command line or IDE who want git and coding-task assistance; teams should also note the feedback-based data collection (via `/bug` and usage data) described in the data policy section.

repos.name: TencentCloud / Octop
repos.description: A smarter, self-hosted AI assistant — multi-user, multi-agent.

summary.goal: Octop is an open-source, self-hosted AI assistant described as multi-user and multi-agent, built for households and small teams. It runs as a single process serving a web dashboard, a CLI, IM channel integrations (Feishu, DingTalk, QQ, WeChat, Telegram, Discord, WeCom), and cron automation, sharing one control-plane database under ~/.octop/ (SQLite by default, PostgreSQL optional).
summary.usage: Installation uses a one-line script, `curl -fsSL https://finnie-1258344699.cos.ap-guangzhou.myqcloud.com/octop/install.sh | bash`, which provisions Python 3.12 via uv with no pre-installed Python required. Next, `octop init` runs an interactive wizard creating the database, JWT secret, and admin account, and `octop run` starts the service, reachable at http://127.0.0.1:8088. Docker deployment is documented via `docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d`.
summary.pros: Documented capabilities include JWT-based multi-user isolation, tool approval and shell command guardrails, PII redaction, pluggable workspace backends (local disk, Docker sandbox, PostgreSQL, or COS/S3), portable memory via the Octop Memory project, and bidirectional ACP support for delegating to external coding agents like OpenCode or Claude Code.
summary.cons: The AgentTeams coordinator feature is labeled Beta and listed as 'in progress' on the roadmap, so its behavior may still change. The documentation also states the host needs a modern multi-core CPU and a few GB of RAM for the process plus model/embedding caches, an operational prerequisite beyond minimal hardware.
summary.fit: Given the stated design goal of keeping conversations, workspaces, and credentials on the user's own machine, Octop appears suited to individuals, families, or small teams seeking a locally hosted, privacy-oriented assistant rather than a cloud-only service.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for AI coding agents that addresses context-window consumption from two sides: raw tool output flooding the context window, and lost session state when a conversation compacts. It runs tool output through sandboxed execution and indexes content into a local SQLite FTS5 knowledge base so only relevant results enter context.
summary.usage: For Claude Code, install with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, restart, then verify with `/context-mode:ctx-doctor`. Other documented clients install via `npm install -g context-mode` plus client-specific MCP/hook configuration. Typing `ctx stats` inside a session shows context savings.
summary.pros: The README reports up to 98% context-size reduction in example scenarios, such as 315 KB of raw session output reduced to roughly 5.4 KB, and a 56 KB Playwright snapshot reduced to under 300 bytes. It states no telemetry, cloud sync, or account requirement, with session data kept in local SQLite files.
summary.cons: Automatic routing enforcement depends on hook support, which the README says varies by platform; platforms without hooks, such as Zed and Antigravity IDE, rely on manually copied instruction files with a documented ~60% compliance rate versus ~98% with hooks enabled. On Linux, Node.js versions below 22.5 are stated as unsupported.
summary.fit: This appears suited to developers using MCP-compatible AI coding agents who want to cut token usage from large tool outputs and preserve task/file state across context compaction. The Elastic License 2.0 allows self-use, forking, and modification but, per the README, disallows offering it as a hosted or managed service.

repos.name: agent-substrate / substrate
repos.description: Agent Substrate: the core system

summary.goal: Agent Substrate is a secure-by-default runtime for running millions of agent sandboxes on Kubernetes, designed to achieve higher density than standard container runtimes while supporting microVM and gVisor sandbox technologies.
summary.usage: The documented quickstart runs `hack/create-kind-cluster.sh` to create a local kind cluster, then `hack/install-ate-kind.sh --deploy-ate-system --credential-provider='{"name":"k8s.io"}'` to install Agent Substrate, PostgreSQL, and rustfs, followed by `kubectl ate create actor my-counter-1 -a ate-demo-counter --template counter` to create an actor for the counter demo.
summary.pros: Documented strengths include framework-agnostic support for ADK, LangChain, Claude Code, CodeX, Antigravity, and MCP agents, along with sub-500ms resume operations, over 500 suspend/resume activations per second, and roughly 10x higher sandbox density.
summary.cons: Agent Substrate is explicitly described as pre-1.0 with no backward-compatibility guarantees, meaning APIs and behavior may change significantly; the bundled credential provider also starts with a default-deny namespace policy, requiring manual grants before actors can receive injected credentials.
summary.fit: Given its reliance on Kubernetes Pods and its early-stage status, Agent Substrate may be best suited for teams already running Kubernetes who can accommodate evolving APIs while experimenting with large-scale agent sandbox workloads.

repos.name: anthropics / knowledge-work-plugins
repos.description: Open source repository of plugins primarily intended for knowledge workers to use in Claude Cowork

summary.goal: Knowledge Work Plugins packages skills, connectors, slash commands, and sub-agents into 11 role-specific plugins (e.g., sales, finance, legal, data) that aim to turn Claude into a specialist for a given job function, built for Claude Cowork and also compatible with Claude Code.
summary.usage: Cowork users install plugins from claude.com/plugins/. Claude Code users first run `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/knowledge-work-plugins`, then `claude plugin install sales@knowledge-work-plugins` (substituting the desired plugin); once installed, skills activate automatically and slash commands like `/sales:call-prep` become available.
summary.pros: Each plugin bundles domain skills that Claude draws on automatically, explicit slash commands, and MCP connectors to external tools; every component is file-based (markdown and JSON), requiring no code, infrastructure, or build steps.
summary.cons: The README describes these plugins as generic starting points that appear to become genuinely useful mainly after customization — editing `.mcp.json` for your tool stack and adding company-specific context to skill files — so out-of-the-box results may be limited until that setup is done.
summary.fit: Appears suited to teams or companies wanting to tailor Claude to their own tools, terminology, and processes across functions like sales, finance, legal, or data, using Claude Cowork or Claude Code.
